claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable solid-solution phase.
High entropy of mixing facilitates formation of a stable solid-solution phase.
Kinetic barriers slow phase separation in high-entropy nanoalloys.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a homogeneous chemical composition.
Heating above 0.5 Tm can induce or reveal phase transformations relevant to the proposed stability mechanism.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the proposed high-temperature comparison.
The relevant structural mediator is formation of a stable solid-solution phase.
High entropy of mixing and kinetic barriers to phase separation constitute the proposed stability mechanism.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will have greater structural stability than a conventional-alloy baseline.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will have greater chemical stability than a conventional-alloy baseline.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will phase-separate more slowly than a conventional-alloy baseline.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will chemically decompose more slowly than a conventional-alloy baseline.
The appropriate baseline is a conventional alloy with similar composition but lower entropy of mixing.
The prediction is bounded to temperatures from 0.5 Tm to 0.8 Tm.
The prediction is bounded to heating rates from 1 to 10 K/min.
Similar or worse structural and chemical stability in the high-entropy nanoalloy relative to the conventional alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
